description: We are an ambitious and diverse team of university and high school students from Tajikistan, united by a profound shared interest in science, technology, space exploration, and continuous learning. Our team is a melting pot of different backgrounds, perspectives, and ideas. While each of our members has unique interests and personal goals, we strongly believe that our differences are our greatest strength. We want to bring these diverse perspectives together to create something truly innovative.
summary: Mars Explorer is an interactive project created by the Stellari team for NASA Space Apps. We combine web development, research, and multilingual storytelling to explore equipment left on the Moon and Mars. Using NASA records, photographs, historical landing coordinates, and panoramic views, visitors discover each mission’s purpose, achievements, and legacy. Our bilingual assistant, TARA, explains information and supports website navigation. We also propose NX1 and NX2: complementary concepts for surface support and underground exploration. NX1 could provide power and communications support, while a tethered NX2 investigates accessible subsurface spaces and returns valuable scientific observations. Addressing “Abandoned but not Forgotten,” our project makes space heritage accessible and explores how future equipment could continue contributing after its original mission or mobility ends.
details:
Mars Explorer, developed by the Stellari team, connects historical space equipment with the stories and discoveries behind it. Visitors explore Moon and Mars landing sites, browse mission records, inspect spacecraft and rover components, and view archival photographs and panoramic scenes.

TARA, our bilingual website assistant, explains project content, reads information aloud, and helps visitors navigate between pages. NX1 and NX2 introduce our proposed concepts for surface support and underground exploration, including a potential second role for equipment after mobility loss. These concepts are educational proposals, not flight-tested hardware.

The website uses React, Vite, JavaScript, React Router, Zustand, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and CSS. It is deployed on Vercel. NASA mission pages, historical landing coordinates, photographs, panoramas, and selected 3D resources support the content. The current version uses a curated catalogue rather than a live NASA API.

Our goal is to make space heritage accessible while encouraging visitors to consider how future missions could preserve scientific value after their original purpose ends.
